items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] Random draw makes Jennifer Thoss Lytton’s mayor after 45-45 tie
items.content_html:

Jennifer Thoss will become mayor of Lytton, British Columbia, after a random draw broke a 45-45 tie with incumbent Denise O’Connor in the Oct. 17 election. A judicial recount at Kamloops Provincial Court on Tuesday confirmed the tally before the draw selected Thoss. Thoss will lead a village rebuilding after a 2021 wildfire that killed two people and destroyed most of its structures. A former councillor, she has criticized the pace of recovery and warned that more than $50 million in planned infrastructure could overwhelm Lytton’s reduced tax base. O’Connor defended the need for recovery staff and infrastructure to attract residents. Thoss said after the draw that she would focus on team-building.

items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] B.C. voters cast ballots in close race as officials hand-count votes
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

British Columbia voters are choosing a 93-member legislature Saturday in a snap provincial election called two years early, with the governing New Democratic Party (NDP) and the Conservative Party of B.C. running close in final polls. During the campaign, Premier David Eby acknowledged frustration over the early election call, while both major parties promoted competing plans on affordability, health care and the economy. Eby initially cited U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade threat as a reason to seek a new mandate, then said he should have explained more clearly that the legislature had stalled under the NDP’s narrow majority. Eby also accused interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson of serving as a “Trojan horse” for extremists in his party; Doerkson called that characterization “absurd”. Election officials will count election-day ballots by hand because the snap vote left Elections BC too little time to prepare enough tabulators. Officials will electronically tabulate advance-voting and electoral-office ballots and report those results first. Absentee and mail-in ballots will not be included in election-night totals; they are scheduled for the final count from Nov. 6 to Nov. 10.

In September, the median listing price fell 1.2% from a year earlier to $419,250, its 11th consecutive annual decline; 21% of listings had an initial price cut, the highest share in four years. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached 7.4% this month, its highest level in nearly three years. Across the 50 largest U.S. metropolitan areas, sellers outnumbered buyers by about 63% last month. The number of buyers was roughly 929,000, the lowest total in records dating to 2013. Sellers are offering money toward repairs, closing costs or lower mortgage payments, but affordability pressures continue to keep prospective buyers on the sidelines.

items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Canadian youth climate trial tests federal emissions policy and constitutional duties
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Canada’s first youth-led federal climate trial opened Oct. 26 in Vancouver, where 15 plaintiffs argue the federal Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act and the 2030 plan fail to cut emissions enough to protect their health and safety. The plaintiffs cite personal harm from heat, wildfire smoke and extreme weather. Canada has warmed about twice as fast as the global average since 1970 and could warm 5 C by century’s end under current global policies, according to federal climate assessments cited in Canadian reporting. Plaintiffs describe smoke-related illness, displacement, flooding and drought. The federal government says Canada cannot guarantee a safe climate on its own, disputes a constitutional duty to do so and argues climate change requires a global response. Witnesses are expected to testify over four to five weeks; closing arguments are scheduled for February 2027, with a decision expected later that year.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN urges steep fossil-fuel cuts as 1.5°C overshoot becomes unavoidable
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 Emissions Gap Report says governments must now limit the scale and duration of global warming beyond 1.5°C, rather than try to prevent that threshold from being crossed. Its lowest-overshoot pathway would cap warming at 1.7°C to 1.8°C around mid-century, with about a 50% chance of returning to 1.5°C by 2100. Following that pathway requires greenhouse-gas emissions to fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, compared with 2025. The report says existing national climate pledges would cut emissions by only 5% to 8% by 2030 and 11% to 15% by 2035. If current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; full delivery of pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. The pathway also calls for sharply reducing coal-fired electricity generation and scaling up carbon removal. The report warns that the required reductions are far beyond current plans. Governments are due to discuss climate action at the COP31 summit, scheduled to open in Antalya on Nov. 9.

items.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [koaa.com] U.S. emissions rise worsens global warming outlook, UN report says
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 emissions assessment says U.S. greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 133 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2025, the largest increase among major economies. The United States accounted for about 70% of the net increase among 124 countries whose emissions grew. The report warns that the world can no longer avoid exceeding the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C threshold and must limit the overshoot. The U.S. increase reflected higher electricity demand and a rebound in coal-fired power generation, while global greenhouse-gas emissions remained roughly level at 58.4 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. The assessment attributes its worsening projections partly to the United States’ formal withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions. Under existing policies, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; fully meeting national climate pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. UNEP says a pathway offering about a 50% chance of limiting peak warming to 1.7–1.8°C and returning to 1.5°C by 2100 requires global emissions cuts of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025. The next UN climate summit, COP31, is scheduled to open in Antalya, Türkiye, next month.

Thousands of people demonstrated across Italy on Saturday, Oct. 24, against rising living costs and war. Police and protesters clashed in Rome, Turin and Bologna, while the Milan march was largely peaceful. Police used tear gas and water cannons in several cities. Authorities said nine people were arrested and 371 were temporarily detained in eight cities, including 110 minors. Demonstrators raised concerns about housing and fuel costs, wages, public services and military spending. Security measures followed the previous weekend’s looting and clashes in Milan, where shops in the fashion district boarded up windows as a precaution. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government sent 500 additional soldiers to Milan and approved tougher measures involving minors. On Saturday, police also detained 30-year-old freelance journalist Youssef Siher, suspected of organizing the 17 October Movement. They searched more than 150 locations in Milan, Monza and about 20 other cities as part of investigations into the earlier unrest.

items.title: [sciencenews.org] Ancient viral DNA silences chimp gene linked to early brain development
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Researchers at Lund University report that DNA left by an ancient retrovirus, PTERV1, silences LINC00662, a gene active in human brain development, in chimpanzees. In lab-grown brain organoids, switching off the gene reduced the activity of genes involved in neuron development and connections; removing the viral sequence from chimpanzee stem cells restored LINC00662 activity. The researchers caution that the experiments cannot establish effects on whole-brain development, abilities or behavior. The study appeared in Science Advances on October 23. The team says it will investigate whether other viral remnants had similar effects and whether such sequences are linked to brain diseases.

items.title: [downes.ca] Principles and Practice of Deep Representation Learning
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Sam Buchanan, Druv Pai, Peng Wang, Yi Ma, GitHub, Oct 22, 2026

This is "a modern fully open-source textbook exploring why and how deep neural networks learn compact and information-dense representations of high-dimensional real-world data." It's a daunting read - and to be honest, I gave the first chapter a careful read but have only skimmed the rest (though it's now on my virtual bookshelf for future reference). I think people who are serious about understanding how we learn and how machines emulate this should at the very least read that first chapter. It contains what is to my understanding an accurate history of artificial intelligence (including the important early work in computation, cybernetics, and information theory). The aim of the book is to give us a framework that explains how neural networks work to generate intelligence. They authors write, "intelligence is not about collecting all informative data in advance and training a model to memorize their (low-dimensional) distribution. Instead, it requires computational mechanisms that can continuously improve current knowledge of the distribution and acquire new information when needed. A fundamental characteristic of any intelligent being or system - whether an animal, a human, a civilization, or the entire scientific community - is the ability to continuously improve or gain new information or knowledge on its own."
